newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, in fighting form, seeks to bury Lenin.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, in fighting form, seeks to bury Lenin.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin dangled a red rag in front of his communist foes in parliament on Friday by suggesting Vladimir Lenin should get a Christian burial.

Yeltsin's government has hinted that he may dissolve parliament if it does not pass its reforms and the 66-year-old president was clearly relishing a new battle when he suggested Russians could decide the fate of the Bolshevik leader's corpse.

"I hope we will gradually rid Red Square of its status of a cemetery," Yeltsin told cultural leaders, saying a referendum could be held in the autumn on whether to move Lenin's mummified body from its polished red marble tomb outside the Kremlin wall.
"The communists, of course, will fight this, but I am used to fighting with them," Yeltsin added.
Yeltsin rarely travels around Russia outside election campaigns and has been busy with foreign policy and a new reform push since he recovered in February from months of illness.
But he was full of fun during his trip to St Petersburg, the start of what he says will be an extensive check on the regions to root out corruption.
"They took my heart, pulled it out and put it back again. Now everything's okay," Yeltsin said, joking about the quintuple heart bypass operation he underwent in November.
"I'm in good, sporting form. That's it. I'm working full strength. The bribe-takers' hands are already shaking," he told a small crowd who turned out to see him in bright summer sunshine.

Courting the intelligensia by chairing a session of his Presidential Council of Culture and Art for the first time, he took another dig at the lower house of parliament or State Duma, which is dominated by opposition communists and nationalists.

"It's a great rarity for us to watch a good play on television," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying. "But at the same time they have live coverage of the Duma. It's funny, but it's stupid."

Communist deputies, who are strongly opposed to the reform push which has accompanied Yeltsin's recovery, lashed out at his government's privatisation policies on Thursday and have stalled a bill slashing spending to offset dismal tax revenues.

They have also tried to control the television coverage which they says shows them in a bad light by focusing on rows, and passed a law banning changes in the appearance of Red Square in a bid to stop Lenin's wax-like corpse from being removed.
But Yeltsin has not signed the law on Red Square and is unlikely to do so.
On Friday he suggested "removing the funereal bloom from Red Square...not with bulldozers or excavators but gradually and in a civilized way," Interfax said.
"This is our history. Let us give it a Christian character. A dead man should not be above earth. He should be buried in earth," Yeltsin told the council.
Yeltsin did not say what he wanted to do with Stalin and other Soviet luminaries buried along the Kremlin wall behind Lenin's tomb.

In a further bid to steal some of his opponents' thunder in case parliamentary elections, which are not due until late 1999, come around sooner, Yeltsin took a dive into high culture, promising money for arts which have withered under his reforms.
He proposed making June 6 a holiday in honour of the birth of the poet Alexander Pushkin in time for its 200th anniversary in 1999.
